Sophocles. An Athenian tragedian from four ninety-six BCE to four hundred six BCE, one of the three great Greek playwrights alongside Aeschylus and Euripides. His surviving plays—Oedipus Rex, Electra, and Antigone, among others—explore the collision between individual will and cosmic destiny, human dignity and fate. His works defined tragic drama and shaped how Western literature treats moral ambiguity and psychological depth.

Sophocles survived nearly ninety years through most of the fifth century BCE, witnessing Athens' rise to power, its wars, and the Peloponnesian conflict. His long life gave him authority as both artist and cultural figure. He won at least eighteen drama competitions at the City Dionysia, Athens' premier theater festival, establishing him as the most celebrated tragedian of his time.

Sophocles authored over one hundred twenty plays during his lifetime. Only seven survive today, making him far better preserved than Aeschylus, whose work predated and influenced his. Oedipus Rex is often considered the perfect tragedy. It turns on the hero's belated discovery that he has already fulfilled the oracle's curse, making him simultaneously victim and agent of his doom. Antigone pits familial loyalty and moral conscience against state law. It stages the conflict between Creon's authoritarian decree and Antigone's sacred duty to bury her brother—a dilemma still debated in ethics and political philosophy.

His plays feature what became the model for Greek tragedy: a protagonist of high status, often blindness—literal or metaphorical—to a terrible truth, and peripeteia, a reversal of fortune triggered by recognition or revelation. Sophocles introduced the third speaking actor to the Greek stage, expanding dramatic possibilities beyond the two-actor limit of Aeschylus' time. This formal innovation allowed greater complexity in characterization and dramatic interaction.

Aeschylus was Sophocles' predecessor and influence. Aeschylus shaped the tragic form that Sophocles refined into philosophical precision. Euripides was his contemporary rival. Where Sophocles emphasized fate and the gods' inscrutability, Euripides questioned divine justice itself. Oedipus Rex became his masterpiece and the model tragedy for centuries. It has been studied for its inevitability and irony ever since. Antigone explores moral conflict between individual conscience and political authority, a perennial question in dramatic art. The plays were performed in Athens during the height of the Athenian empire and democracy's flourishing. The Oresteia by Aeschylus set the template for tragic structure that Sophocles inherited and perfected. Later dramatists like William Shakespeare echoed Sophocles' exploration of tragic flaw and fate.
